E0436.summary: In Sendivogius, what the living metals are to be made into in Our Fire; the text does not explain it further.
E0436.body: Quoted from Sendivogius: of the living metals “let there be made of them a dry liquor” [IV.3 ¶21], in connection with Our Fire. The text gives no further explanation.

E0437.summary: Atwood's term for the soul that has left nature and its moisture, turns to itself and radiates its own light; Heraclitus calls it the wisest.
E0437.body: Atwood describes the soul that has withdrawn from nature and its moisture: turning to itself, it radiates its own light — “then she becomes a dry splendor from exhalation” [II.3 ¶27]. She cites Heraclitus: “a dry soul is the wisest” [II.3 ¶27].

E0438.summary: A philosophers' name for the 'living water' that the Stone is; also one of the forms the subject takes in its changes.
E0438.body: Quoted from Geber, dry water is the philosophers' name for the living water that the Stone is: “living water, which we have named dry water” [I.2 ¶11] (= living water). Atwood herself lists *aqua sicca* among the forms the subject takes in its mutations — “a stone, a vapor, or an aqua sicca” [I.2 ¶37] — without further explanation.

forms: dry water of the sea of the wise
E0439.summary: In Eudoxus, that with which the extracted water is joined by a 'magical union', dissolving it into the viscous mercurial liquor.
E0439.body: Quoted from Eudoxus: the extracted water is dissolved into the viscous mercurial liquor “by a magical union of the dry water of the sea of the wise” [IV.3 ¶16]. The text does not explain the expression further.

E0440.summary: Cited for his English verse rendering (Aeneid, lib. 6) of a Latin passage Atwood quotes.
E0440.body: Atwood gives Dryden's English verse from his Aeneid, lib. 6, as a rendering of the Latin quoted in the same paragraph: “Deep forests and impenetrable night Possess the middle space” [II.3 ¶6; II.3 n3].

E0441.summary: The generating pair: if the divine Idea brought forth directly in it, the offspring would be imperfect and discordant; in the oracle it sits beside the Monad.
E0441.body: Atwood treats the Duad as the generating pair: “For if in the Duad the divine Idea were suffered immediately to bring forth, an imperfect offspring would result” [IV.2 ¶20] — imperfect and discordant through the predominance of either extreme. In the oracle she cites, the Duad stands beside the Monad: “For the Duad sits beside him and glitters with intellectual sections,” [IV.2 ¶22].

E0442.summary: Reflective contemplation, which is excluded, together with multitude, when Matter is called 'one so far as one'.
E0442.body: Atwood glosses dual contemplation as reflective contemplation (= reflective contemplation): Matter is called one so far as one by “depriving the idea of multitude and dual, i.e., reflective, contemplation” [III.2 ¶52].

E0443.summary: Author of the Histoire Hermetique, cited for a skeptic's praise of English Hermetic writers and for Lully material, yet criticized as ignorant of the subject.
E0443.body: Atwood cites his Histoire Hermetique several times. As a skeptic's testimony to English Hermetic writing she quotes: “les Anglois n’ecrivent sur la science hermetique avec beaucoup de lumiere et de profondeur” [I.1 ¶72; I.1 n92] (our rendering: the English write on the hermetic science with much light and depth). He is cited in support of the Lully story; his catalogue lists about 200 of Lully's alchemical treatises; and he is a reference for the laws forbidding transmutation [I.1 ¶47; I.1 ¶48; I.1 n58; I.1 n61]. He is also cited (vol. 2) for transmutation stories [I.1 n104]. But Atwood criticizes his Catalogue (tom. iii, Paris, 1762): he reduced the count of authors, was ignorant of the subject, and excluded writers by title rather than matter [I.1 ¶75; I.1 n97].

E0444.summary: In the quoted fraternity of the Rosy Cross, one of two mutually devouring yet loving creatures; tortured, it yields tears, and its 'embers' are obtained at the second gate.
E0444.body: Quoted from the fraternity of the Rosy Cross: the Eagle is one of two creatures that devour yet love each other; tortured, it weeps — “Torture the Eagle till she weeps” [III.3 ¶63] — and its embers are obtained at the second gate. The text gives no plain meaning.

E0445.summary: Group voices cited together as agreeing that the Mysteries were instituted pure and for the noblest ends.
E0445.body: Atwood cites them in support of the original purity of the Mysteries: “early Christians concurring with the wisest Ethnics in declaring that they proposed the noblest ends” [II.4 ¶56].

E0446.summary: For Atwood, the crucible for souls as well as bodies; in Hermes, 'our earth', the body of spirit and soul, the feminine earth of the masculine.
E0446.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says “the earth is the crucible for souls as well as bodies” [APP ¶110]; it is that into which power is turned to be made integral, and “this earth becomes the punctum saliens of the Divine Cross which before was its punctum” [APP ¶110].

In the quoted Hermes, 'our earth' has sulphur as its fatness; the earth begot between water (spirit) and redness (soul) is the body of both — “the earth begot betwixt them is the substance or body of both” [I.3 n21] (= substance or body of both); “the feminine is the earth of the masculine” [I.3 ¶22]; and Magnesia is sown in the Philosophic Earth. Earth is also identified with the residue: “the faeces or earth which remains below” [I.3 ¶23] (= faeces).

E0447.summary: In the sage's saying 'visit the interior of the earth', Atwood reads the earth as our chaotic sense-life, not soil.
E0447.body: Atwood interprets the sage's saying “Visit the interior of the earth rectifying” [II.3 ¶29]: the earth meant is “not the feculent dead soil, but our dark divulsed chaotic life from sense” [II.3 ¶29] (= our dark divulsed chaotic life from sense).

E0448.summary: The Hermetists' earth, located within their heaven and named so to distinguish it from the 'feculent dead soil'.
E0448.body: Atwood says the Hermetists place their earth within their heaven and “call it magical, the Earth of the Wise, Olympus, Our Earth” [III.2 ¶36] (= magical earth, Olympus, Our Earth), “in order to distinguish from the feculent dead soil” [III.2 ¶36].

E0449.summary: In the Benedictine Monk, the vessel containing fire, air and water in the work, glossed as the gross body or composition.
E0449.body: Quoted from the Benedictine Monk: fire, air and water are contained “in their earthly vessel, i.e., in their gross body or composition” [III.3 ¶24] (= gross body or composition).

E0450.summary: Named as the places and celebrants of the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries.
E0450.body: Atwood names the Eastern temples and the priests at Eleusis as where the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries were celebrated [II.2 ¶24].

E0451.summary: A source cited in footnotes for honoring the physician and for Wisdom's secret being with the Faithful.
E0451.body: Cited (Eccles. 8; Idem., 1) in support of honoring the physician and of the saying that Wisdom's secret belongs to the Faithful: “Her secret is with the Faithful” [IV.3 ¶36; IV.3 n14; IV.3 n15].

E0452.summary: Cited (1:6-8) in support of Wisdom as created by God, poured on all his works and given to those who love him.
E0452.body: Atwood cites Ecclesiasticus 1:6-8 on Wisdom: “He created her and numbered her, and poured her out upon all his works.” [III.3 ¶48; III.3 n33] — and given to those who love him.

E0453.summary: Cited in the Appendix in support of the change in the blood wrought by reiterated contritions.
E0453.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Eckhartshausen is cited in support of the change in the blood wrought by reiterative contritions [APP ¶78].

E0454.summary: Atwood's term for the active, working cause within the total essence, to be drawn forth, known in co-identity, and related to mind rather than generative life.
E0454.body:
Atwood uses the Efficient for the active cause the method seeks to recover. It is to be drawn forth from within: the aim is to “draw forth the true Efficient and to know it in co-identity” [II.3 ¶5]. It lies in the intelligible substance of reason's Law: “For there the true Efficient is to be found, which is not externally developed” [II.3 ¶46]. Knowledge and the efficient rise together: “It is from within that the knowledge springs together with the true efficient” [III.1 ¶40], the two “which are indeed one in principle” [III.1 ¶40] (= knowledge), though distinguished in practice for the sake of offspring. The “Rational Efficient, armed with a bright intelligence” [III.1 ¶47] discovers the evil of its first conception and dissolves the Vital Bond; the text does not explicitly say this is the same as the 'true efficient'.

In the dissolution, “the newly roused Efficient is exceeding wrathful” [III.1 ¶56], reducing the body of Light (Osiris) to vapor. It is universal: there is “not the smallest grain of sand without the Efficient which is in all” [III.2 ¶43], and without it numbers and figures produce nothing substantive. One who mingles with it keeps a remnant of it: “whoever thus becomes One by mingling with the Efficient, will have a remnant of it with himself” [III.2 ¶66]. The Platonic Successor, quoted, calls it the soul's cause: “the soul, being in such a condition, associates with her Efficient” [III.3 ¶26], gaining a similitude of it. Once Mind attains Self Knowledge, “the Efficient proceeds out wards to image its motive in operation” [IV.1 ¶48].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says this life-power is now dislocated downward: “The Efficient must be regained. That is, it is to be related to mind and not to the generative life.” [APP ¶134].

E0455.summary: Atwood's name, in the Appendix, for Causality, of which we ordinarily have no experience; contact with universal power initiates regenerate life.
E0455.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood equates it with Causality: “We know noting of Causality --- i.e., we have no experience of the Efficient Power.” [APP ¶175] (= Causality). The individual mind's contact with power universal initiates regenerate life [APP ¶175].

E0456.summary: In Khunrath, something in vegetables that the Stone increases; not further defined.
E0456.body: Quoted from Khunrath: the Stone acts on “vegetables, by an increase of their efflorescent spirit” [IV.3 ¶28]. Not further defined.

E0457.summary: In Hermes, 'our egg' holds the one disposition sought; the hen's egg is the nearest natural analogue to the art's compound simple.
E0457.body: Quoted from Hermes: 'our egg' holds the one disposition sought. The hen's egg, made of four elements, is the closest natural analogue, “which answers in all respects, excepting the catholicity, to the compound simple of this art” [I.3 n26].

E0458.summary: Atwood's name for the subject when it is 'nothing': a formless, potential state amid its mutations.
E0458.body: Atwood says the subject, among its mutations, is at one stage nothing “but a potential chaos and egg of philosophers” [I.2 ¶37] (= potential chaos).

forms: Egyptian Fable of Isis and Osiris
E0459.summary: Cited to illustrate Intellect bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring, represented by the birth of Horus.
E0459.body: Atwood uses the fable to illustrate Intellect bringing itself into natural effect by begetting a supernatural offspring; the birth of Horus represents the metaphysical offspring [IV.2 ¶6; IV.2 ¶7; IV.2 ¶11].

forms: Egyptian Mythology of Isis and Osiris
E0460.summary: The mythology Synesius is said to explain with the enigma of the two pairs of eyes.
E0460.body: Named as the mythology that Synesius is said to explain by the enigma of the two pairs of eyes [III.1 ¶45].

E0461.summary: Cited to illustrate the rebellious Principle depicted in human form with emblems of grace and power, seated between his foes.
E0461.body: Atwood cites Egyptian relics as depicting the rebellious Principle in human semblance, with emblems of grace and power, seated between his foes [III.1 ¶64].

E0462.summary: Cited approvingly for teaching self-knowledge and placing the Sphinx before Isis, but in the Appendix criticized as an example of self-willed magic.
E0462.body: Atwood cites the Egyptians in support of the precept “that Man should know himself” [II.1 ¶39], meant experimentally and ontologically. They placed the Sphinx in the vestibule of Isis, which she reads as Ether guarding Wisdom [III.1 ¶5]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) they are criticized as an example of the magic of the self-will: their magicians' “enchantments” drew only on their own strength, and so Egypt fell [APP ¶2; APP ¶4; APP ¶5].

E0463.summary: In Poemander's account given by Hermes, Intellect, reached when the ascending part is stripped of all operations; above it powers sing praises to God.
E0463.body: Quoted from Poemander in Hermes' account: the ascending part, naked of all operations, “cometh to the eighth sphere, which is Intellect” [III.3 ¶57] (= Intellect); above it are powers singing praises to God.

E0464.summary: The adept Atwood calls the most celebrated later adept and a 'perfect artist'; she draws heavily on his verse and prose for fire, matter, operations, multiplication and projection.
E0464.body:
Atwood presents Eirenaeus Philalethes as the most celebrated later adept, a perfect artist whose identity is unknown, listing works including An Open Entrance to the Shut Palace of the King, Ripley Revived and The Marrow of Alchemy [I.1 ¶73]; he is the 'foregoing' adept with whom Vaughan is confounded [I.1 ¶74]. She qualifies his Ripley Revived as practically explanatory for the initiated but sophistical to beginners [I.1 ¶64; I.1 n67], and quotes him that “our books are made for those who have been or intend to become conversant about the search of nature” [I.2 ¶50; I.2 n50]. He is among adepts warning against practice before full understanding [I.1 ¶86]; “Few, very few, Philalethes said, there were in his day” [II.2 ¶25] who understood the principle.

On the agent: “This Form is Light, the source of central heat” [I.2 ¶45; I.2 n44]; nature's one secret agent — “For she her secret agent doth possess, Which in the universe is only one” [II.2 ¶28; II.2 n19]; “Our fire is the true sulfur of Gold” [III.1 ¶13]; “For in our water is our secret fire.” [III.1 ¶69; III.1 n73]. He supplies the account of fire, waters, menstruals, regimen and signs [III.1 ¶14]. Atwood finds 'a profound mystery' in “To Saturn, Mars with bond of love is tied,” [III.1 ¶58; III.1 n64]. Other uses: “Separate, says Eiraneaus, the light from the darkness seven times” [I.3 n39]; “Never grudge, then, that thou hast destroyed thye gold” [III.3 ¶22; III.3 n12], glossed as the first fruits of reason; the one key — “That ‘t is a fountain sealed, Which one thing only can unlocke;” [III.3 ¶67; III.3 n46]; the gross understanding's false light — “that darkness I now perceived had a false fore of its own” [III.4 ¶16; III.4 n11].

On practice: “there is no work more tedious than our First Operation” [IV.1 ¶6; IV.1 n5], distinct from the Second, where Nature works alone [IV.1 ¶11]; two contrary works done apart then reconciled — “For what one doth concoct t’other will drive away;” [IV.1 ¶42; IV.1 n37]; a favored case — “of a vulgar ignoramus I became a true Adept” [IV.1 ¶17; IV.1 n18]. For multiplication and projection: “But one at last ting’d ninety thousand more” [IV.3 ¶25; IV.3 n6]; “you will no longer be able to calculate the strength of the medicine” [IV.3 ¶18; IV.3 ¶20; IV.3 n1] — the text attributes ¶18 to the Author of the Open Entrance and ¶20 to E. Philalethes' Introitus Apertus without stating they are one. He is cited for a universal medicine — “even one Adept, were he permitted, might impart health to the whole world” [IV.3 ¶26; IV.3 n7] — after which Atwood tells gold-seekers to disregard such testimony. Within the Adept's words he is cited for the menstruum in the sphere of Saturn that can calcine gold, identified with the Salt [IV.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), “Take that matter which is gold” [APP ¶89] is glossed as finding the magical earth at one's own center. Whether 'the Cosmopolite Eirenaeus' [III.1 ¶64] is a further source or a co-source of the Lion Hunt poem is unclear.

E0465.summary: In Norton, the chosen astrological arrangement for the work, which the operator's nativity may contradict.
E0465.body: Quoted from Norton: the Election is the chosen astrological arrangement for the work, which the operator's own nativity may oppose — “In contrariety of this Election” [IV.2 ¶34].
